title: Bhuvan Bam Picks Up the Clapboard for Dhindora 2. The YouTube Kid Who Crossed 500 Million Views Now Has Netflix Holding the Camera.
excerpt: Season 1 was a one-man show shot for his own channel. Season 2 is a Netflix production across Punjab, Delhi and Mumbai — and Titu Mama is finally getting the spotlight.
body:
The photo is almost defiantly simple: a man on a set, holding a clapboard that reads "Dhindora 2 Filming Now." No glossy poster, no orchestral teaser. Just **Bhuvan Bam** and a caption that could only come from him — "Nayi Chunauti, Naya Mehmaan, Naya Dhindora! Netflix and I need your blessings. Peet do Dhindora!!"

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=IUsiTOUo3HE</youtube>

If you grew up on Indian YouTube, that single image hits differently. Because the story behind that clapboard is one of the most improbable rise narratives in modern Indian entertainment, and it just entered its biggest chapter yet.

https://x.com/hajarkagalwa/status/2068543168774390032

Rewind to 2015. Bhuvan Bam was a kid making sketch videos in his bedroom, playing every character himself — the nagging mother, the foul-mouthed friend, the exhausted father — on a channel called **BB Ki Vines**. No studio, no godfather, no film-family surname. Just a phone, a sense of comic timing, and an instinct for the absurd rhythms of middle-class Indian life. He became, by sheer accumulation of views and devotion, one of the country's first true creator-celebrities.

Then in 2021 he gambled. He poured everything into **Dhindora**, a scripted series released not on a streaming platform but on his own YouTube channel — a genuine indie production. It reportedly crossed 500 million views. Five hundred million. That's not a web series; that's a cultural event that happened to live on YouTube. It proved a creator could mount a full scripted show, multi-character and all, and command an audience most studios would kill for.

Netflix noticed. And now the giant has come calling.

**Dhindora 2** — announced earlier this year as part of Netflix India's 2026 slate at the *Next On Netflix* showcase — has officially begun filming. The contrast with Season 1 is the whole story. What was once an independent passion project released for free is now a Netflix India production, mounted on a significantly larger scale. The shoot kicked off in **Punjab** and will travel to **Delhi** and **Mumbai**, directed by **Sneha Shetty Kohli**, with Bam co-producing alongside Rohit Raj and cinematography by Georgy John.

> "Nayi Chunauti, Naya Mehmaan, Naya Dhindora! Netflix and I need your blessings. Peet do Dhindora!!" — Bhuvan Bam

Here's the detail fans have been waiting for: Season 2 will reportedly lean hard into **Titu Mama**, the breakout character from the franchise, and Bam is set to play around ten different roles this time. The one-man-universe gimmick that built BB Ki Vines isn't being sanded down for the big platform — it's being scaled up. There's also buzz that veteran comic actor **Rajpal Yadav** could join the cast, which would be a delicious pairing: India's most reliable scene-stealer dropped into Bam's chaotic, lovingly grimy world.

And the timing tells you everything about where Bam's career is right now. He wrapped his big-screen debut **Kuku Ki Kundali** — a rom-com opposite **Wamiqa Gabbi**, directed by Sharan Sharma — and moved into Dhindora 2 within days. He's also part of the pre-Independence drama **The Revolutionaries** and has a Dharma Productions film, announced with Karan Johar himself. The bedroom-sketch kid is now juggling Netflix, a theatrical lead, and a Dharma banner simultaneously. Filmmaker Nikkhil Advani recently compared his work ethic to Shah Rukh Khan, Salman Khan and Akshay Kumar — and for once, the comparison doesn't feel like hype inflation.

For the diaspora, the Dhindora universe is a specific kind of comfort food. Bam's humour is untranslatable in the best way — it lives in the texture of Hindi-speaking households, the aunties and the uncles and the WhatsApp-forward logic of family life. For NRIs raising kids on Marvel and Minecraft, a Netflix-backed Dhindora 2 is a way to beam that very particular flavour of home into living rooms in New Jersey and Leicester, with subtitles ready and the platform already on the TV. When it drops — expected sometime next year — it'll be a click away, no VPN, no grey-market stream.

The boy who once needed your subscribe now has Netflix's logo on his clapboard. But the message under it is the same one he's been making since 2015: stick around, the chaos is just getting started. Peet do Dhindora, indeed.
